items.explanation: PLAX is read from the transducer down: RV, septum, LV with the mitral valve, LV posterior wall; the septum continues into the anterior aortic wall and the anterior mitral leaflet into the posterior aortic wall, with the LA behind the aortic root and the descending aorta behind the LA.

markers.why: The chamber nearest the transducer (top of the picture) is the RV, here its outflow portion, in front of the septum.
The septum lies between RV (above) and LV (below) and continues into the anterior wall of the aortic root; its end-diastolic thickness is measured here.
The aortic valve sits in the aortic root on the right of the screen; PLAX shows the right coronary cusp anteriorly and usually the non-coronary cusp posteriorly, closed in diastole.
The longer mitral leaflet, hinged on the posterior wall of the aortic root (aorto-mitral continuity); it forms the posterior border of the LV outflow tract.
The left atrium lies behind the aortic root on the right of the screen; its anteroposterior diameter is measured here.
The bottom wall of the LV, behind the posterior mitral leaflet; with the septum it gives LV wall thickness and relative wall thickness.

The circle behind the LA, posterior to the pericardial reflection (the coronary sinus lies in front of it, in the AV groove): a pericardial effusion tracks in front of it, a left pleural effusion behind it.

items.concept: Echo anatomy: parasternal short-axis view, aortic valve level
items.explanation: The aortic valve sits in the middle with the RVOT wrapping around it from the tricuspid valve (left of the screen) to the pulmonary valve (right). Right coronary cusp anterior, left coronary cusp next to the pulmonary artery, non-coronary cusp next to the interatrial septum.

markers.why: The anterior cusp, facing the RV outflow tract.
The cusp on the right of the screen (the patient's left), next to the pulmonary artery; the left main coronary artery arises from its sinus.
The cusp on the left of the screen, next to the interatrial septum and the right atrium.
The RV outflow tract wraps anteriorly around the aortic valve from the tricuspid valve (left) to the pulmonary valve (right).
The valve at the end of the RVOT on the right of the screen, in front of the aortic valve; the main pulmonary artery runs beyond it.
The valve on the left of the screen between the RA and the RV inflow.
The chamber behind the aortic valve (bottom of the picture), separated from the RA by the interatrial septum.

items.source: Mitchell C, et al. Guidelines for performing a comprehensive transthoracic echocardiographic examination in adults (ASE). J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2019;32:1-64

items.concept: Echo anatomy: parasternal short-axis view, mitral level and coronary territories
items.explanation: Viewed from the apex, the LV is a ring with the fish-mouth mitral orifice inside and the RV crescent anterior and to the left of the screen. Going clockwise from the top: anterior (LAD), anterolateral, inferolateral (usually LCx), inferior (usually RCA), inferoseptal and anteroseptal segments.

markers.why: The crescent-shaped RV wraps around the circular LV, anterior and to the left of the screen.
The LV wall shared with the RV, on the left of the screen (anteroseptal and inferoseptal segments).
The upper (anterior) lip of the fish-mouth orifice; planimetry at the leaflet tips gives the mitral valve area in mitral stenosis.
The lower (posterior) lip of the fish-mouth orifice.
The top of the LV ring: the anterior wall, LAD territory.
The bottom of the LV ring, beside the inferoseptum: the inferior wall, usually RCA territory.
Lower right of the LV ring: the inferolateral (formerly posterior) wall, usually circumflex territory.

items.explanation: In the ASE orientation the apex is at the top, the LV on the right and the RV on the left, atria at the bottom. The morphological RV is the one with the moderator band and the more apically inserted atrioventricular valve (the tricuspid).

markers.why: The ventricle on the right of the screen (ASE orientation): longer than the RV, it forms the true apex.
The smaller, triangular ventricle on the left of the screen; its apex meets the septum below the LV apex.
The atrium at the bottom right, behind the mitral valve; its volume is traced at end-systole.
The atrium at the bottom left, behind the tricuspid valve.
The valve between LA and LV; its septal insertion is slightly further from the apex than the tricuspid's.
The valve between RA and RV; its septal leaflet inserts slightly closer to the apex than the mitral, a marker of the morphological RV (displacement ≥ 8 mm/m² suggests Ebstein anomaly).
The muscular band across the RV apex from the septum to the free wall; it carries the right bundle branch and identifies the morphological RV.

items.source: Mitchell C, et al. Guidelines for performing a comprehensive transthoracic echocardiographic examination in adults (ASE). J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2019;32:1-64

items.title: Label the apical four-chamber view (A4C)

items.explanation: Rotating the probe about 60 degrees anticlockwise from A4C removes the right heart: only LV and LA remain, with the inferior wall on the left and the anterior wall on the right of the screen, the left atrial appendage on the anterior side and the coronary sinus in the inferior AV groove.

markers.why: The only ventricle in this view: A2C shows no RV and no septum.
The atrium at the bottom; its area here and in A4C gives the biplane LA volume.
The valve between LA and LV, open in diastole.
The LV wall on the left of the screen in A2C: the inferior wall, usually RCA territory.
The LV wall on the right of the screen in A2C: the anterior wall, LAD territory.
The pouch off the LA on the anterior side; transthoracic echo cannot exclude a thrombus here (TEE is needed).
The small circle in the left AV groove near the inferior mitral annulus; a dilated coronary sinus suggests a persistent left superior vena cava.

items.source: Mitchell C, et al. Guidelines for performing a comprehensive transthoracic echocardiographic examination in adults (ASE). J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2019;32:1-64

items.title: Label the apical two-chamber view (A2C)

items.explanation: Tilting the A4C anteriorly brings the LV outflow tract, aortic valve and aortic root (the fifth chamber) into the middle of the picture, between the basal septum and the anterior mitral leaflet. It is the view for LVOT pulsed-wave and aortic continuous-wave Doppler.

markers.why: The ventricle on the right of the screen, as in A4C.
The septum; its basal part bounds the LV outflow tract, and basal septal hypertrophy narrows it in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
The outflow tract between the basal septum and the anterior mitral leaflet; pulsed-wave Doppler here gives the LVOT VTI (stroke volume, continuity equation).
The valve at the start of the aortic root in the middle of the picture; continuous-wave Doppler through it gives the aortic jet velocity and gradients.
The aortic root, the fifth chamber, leaving the LV between the atria when the A4C is tilted anteriorly.
The leaflet hinged on the posterior wall of the aortic root; its systolic anterior motion obstructs the LV outflow tract in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
The atrium behind and to the right of the aortic root.

items.source: Mitchell C, et al. Guidelines for performing a comprehensive transthoracic echocardiographic examination in adults (ASE). J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2019;32:1-64

items.concept: LV systolic function: biplane Simpson EF, indexed LV volume, ESC HF categories
items.explanation: The biplane method of discs (modified Simpson's rule) is the recommended 2-D method because it does not assume a shape: it sums 20 elliptical discs traced in A4C and A2C. Pitfalls: apical foreshortening (underestimates volumes), endocardial dropout (use contrast when two or more contiguous segments are not seen) and tracing the trabeculae instead of the compacted myocardium. LVEF ≤ 35% despite at least 3 months of optimal medical therapy is the threshold the ESC 2021 HF guideline uses for primary-prevention ICD consideration in ischaemic cardiomyopathy, so the number is worth re-measuring carefully (or by contrast echo / CMR) when it is near 35%.

fields.label: LVEF (biplane)
fields.why: EF = (EDV - ESV) / EDV = (176 - 118) / 176 = 58 / 176 = 33%. Stroke volume = 58 mL.

fields.label: Indexed LV end-diastolic volume
fields.why: 176 / 1.85 = 95 mL/m². The ASE/EACVI 2015 upper limit is about 74 mL/m² in men (61 in women): the LV is dilated, i.e. remodelled after the infarct.

fields.label: LVEF category (ESC 2021 heart failure)
fields.why: 33% is ≤ 40%: HF with reduced EF. The ESC 2021 bands are ≤ 40%, 41-49% and ≥ 50%.

fields.label: Conclusion

options.label: Normal LV size and systolic function
Dilated LV with LVEF in the mildly reduced range (41-49%)
Dilated LV with LVEF ≤ 35% after 3 months of therapy

fields.why: EDVi 95 mL/m² (dilated) and LVEF 33% (≤ 35%) measured after at least 3 months of guideline-directed therapy.

measurements.label: Regional wall motion
measurements.value: Akinetic apex and distal anterior wall

items.title: LV volumes and ejection fraction by the biplane method of discs

items.concept: Diastolic function: ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithm 2, mitral inflow pattern, LAVI
items.explanation: Under ASE/EACVI 2016, choosing the algorithm comes first: algorithm 1 asks whether diastolic function is abnormal in a normal heart (septal e' < 7 or lateral e' < 10 cm/s, average E/e' > 14, TR > 2.8 m/s, LAVI > 34 mL/m²; more than half positive = dysfunction), algorithm 2 estimates LA pressure when the myocardium is already abnormal. In algorithm 2, E/A ≤ 0.8 with E ≤ 50 cm/s means grade I and normal LA pressure; E/A ≥ 2 means grade III; anything in between needs the three criteria (E/e' > 14, TR > 2.8 m/s, LAVI > 34 mL/m²). The reduced septal e' (6 cm/s) confirms impaired relaxation but is not one of the algorithm 2 criteria. Dated note: this item follows ASE/EACVI 2016. The ASE 2025 update (Nagueh et al.) uses one algorithm for every LVEF: e', E/e' and TR velocity (or PASP) come first, and LAVI, LA strain, pulmonary vein flow and IVRT are used only when these disagree; grading is then by E/A. Applying it gives the same grade for this patient.

fields.label: Which ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithm applies?

options.label: Algorithm 1: normal LVEF, no myocardial disease (four criteria for diastolic dysfunction)
Algorithm 2: reduced LVEF, or normal LVEF with myocardial disease (estimate LA pressure and grade)
Algorithm 1 first; algorithm 2 only if more than half of its four criteria are positive

fields.why: LV hypertrophy is myocardial disease (13 mm walls and an LV mass index of 112 g/m², above the ASE/EACVI 2015 limit of 95 g/m² for women), so the filling-pressure algorithm (2) is used directly even though the LVEF is normal. Algorithm 1 is for a structurally normal heart with normal LVEF: it asks whether diastolic function is abnormal at all.

fields.label: LA volume index
fields.why: 54 / 1.80 = 30 mL/m², below the 34 mL/m² cut-off.

fields.label: Mitral inflow branch of algorithm 2

options.label: E/A ≤ 0.8 with E > 50 cm/s, or E/A > 0.8 but < 2

fields.why: E/A 0.6 and E 45 cm/s: the first branch, which gives normal LA pressure and grade I directly; the three supporting criteria are not needed.

fields.label: Estimated LA pressure
fields.why: The low E/A, low E branch means normal mean LA pressure; the other data agree (septal E/e' 45 / 6 = 7.5; TR 2.3 m/s; LAVI 30 mL/m²).

fields.label: Conclusion

options.label: Grade I diastolic dysfunction (impaired relaxation), normal LA pressure
Grade II diastolic dysfunction, elevated LA pressure

fields.why: Impaired relaxation (low E, tall A, long DT, low septal e') with a normal filling pressure.

items.concept: Diastolic function: ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithm 2, three supporting criteria, pseudonormal filling
items.explanation: A pseudonormal inflow (E/A 1.4, DT 170 ms) looks like a normal one: the clue is the low e' and the high E/e', and the large LA and raised TR velocity confirm that the LA pressure is high. In algorithm 2 the middle inflow branch is resolved by E/e' > 14 (septal > 15 or lateral > 13 when only one annulus is available), TR > 2.8 m/s and LAVI > 34 mL/m². A Valsalva manoeuvre that lowers E/A by 50% or more also unmasks pseudonormal filling. In reduced LVEF, raised filling pressure means a congested patient: titrate diuretics and treat the cause. Dated note: this item follows ASE/EACVI 2016. The ASE 2025 update (Nagueh et al.) uses one algorithm for every LVEF: e', E/e' and TR velocity (or PASP) come first, and LAVI, LA strain, pulmonary vein flow and IVRT are used only when these disagree; grading is then by E/A. Applying it gives the same grade for this patient.

fields.label: Mitral inflow branch of algorithm 2

options.label: E/A ≤ 0.8 with E > 50 cm/s, or E/A > 0.8 but < 2

fields.why: E/A 1.4 lies between 0.8 and 2, so the inflow alone cannot tell normal from raised LA pressure: check the three criteria.

fields.label: LA volume index
fields.why: 78 / 1.95 = 40 mL/m², above 34 mL/m².

fields.label: Number of positive ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithm 2 criteria (of E/e', TR velocity, LAVI)
fields.why: Septal E/e' 17 > 15 (the septal-only cut-off; > 14 when averaged), TR 3.0 > 2.8 m/s and LAVI 40 > 34 mL/m²: three of three.

fields.label: Estimated LA pressure
fields.why: Two or three positive criteria mean elevated LA pressure; two or three negative mean normal; one of two (when only two are available) is indeterminate.

fields.label: Conclusion

options.label: Grade I diastolic dysfunction, normal LA pressure
Grade II diastolic dysfunction (pseudonormal filling), elevated LA pressure

fields.why: E/A < 2 with raised LA pressure is grade II; grade III needs E/A ≥ 2.

items.concept: Aortic stenosis: Vmax, mean gradient, AVA by continuity equation, DVI, stroke volume index
items.explanation: Continuity equation: flow through the LVOT equals flow through the valve, so AVA = LVOT area x LVOT VTI / aortic VTI. The LVOT diameter is squared, so a 1 mm error changes the AVA by about 10%; the DVI (velocity or VTI ratio) avoids it. ASE/EACVI 2017 severe AS: Vmax ≥ 4 m/s, mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg, AVA < 1.0 cm² (indexed < 0.6 cm²/m²), DVI < 0.25. Here AVAi is 0.71 / 1.80 = 0.39 cm²/m². A symptomatic patient with severe high-gradient AS needs valve intervention (SAVR or TAVI, chosen by the Heart Team).

fields.label: AVA by continuity equation
fields.why: LVOT area = π x (2.1/2)² = 3.46 cm²; AVA = 3.46 x 20 / 97 = 0.71 cm² (severe: < 1.0 cm²).

fields.label: Dimensionless index (LVOT VTI / aortic VTI)
fields.why: 20 / 97 = 0.21 (severe: < 0.25). It needs no LVOT diameter, so it avoids the squared diameter error.

fields.label: Stroke volume index
fields.why: SV = 3.46 x 20 = 69 mL; 69 / 1.80 = 38 mL/m², above 35 mL/m²: normal flow, so the gradient is valid.

fields.label: Grading consistency

options.label: Concordant: velocity, gradient, AVA and DVI all in the severe range
Discordant: small AVA with a low gradient
Not assessable without a CT calcium score

fields.why: Vmax ≥ 4 m/s, mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg, AVA < 1.0 cm² and DVI < 0.25 agree.

fields.label: Conclusion
fields.why: All criteria are concordant for severe AS with normal flow; with symptoms this is an indication for valve intervention.

items.source: ASE/EACVI 2017 aortic stenosis update (Baumgartner et al., J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2017;30:372-392); ESC/EACTS 2021 valvular heart disease (Vahanian et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:561-632); ESC/EACTS 2025 valvular heart disease (Praz et al., Eur Heart J 2025, doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194): the thresholds here are the 2021 values

items.title: Aortic stenosis: continuity equation

items.concept: Aortic stenosis: classical low-flow low-gradient AS, stroke volume index, dobutamine stress echo
items.explanation: Flow caveat: gradients fall with flow, so a low gradient does not exclude severe AS when the stroke volume is low. In classical low-flow, low-gradient AS (reduced LVEF) low-dose dobutamine echo raises flow: true severe AS keeps a small AVA (≤ 1.0 cm²) while the mean gradient rises to ≥ 40 mmHg; pseudo-severe AS opens up (AVA rises above 1.0 cm²) with little gradient rise. An SV rise < 20% means no flow (contractile) reserve, and then a CT calcium score helps. With preserved LVEF the same discordance is paradoxical low-flow AS, assessed with the CT calcium score.

fields.label: Stroke volume index
fields.why: LVOT area = π x 1.0² = 3.14 cm²; SV = 3.14 x 14 = 44 mL; 44 / 1.85 = 24 mL/m², well under 35 mL/m²: low flow.

fields.label: Grading consistency

options.label: Discordant: AVA < 1.0 cm² but mean gradient < 40 mmHg, with low flow
Concordant severe: no further test needed
Concordant moderate: the small AVA is a measurement error

fields.why: The gradient depends on flow: a weak LV pushing 44 mL cannot generate 40 mmHg even through a tight valve, but a weak LV may also fail to open a moderately diseased valve fully.

fields.label: Conclusion and next step

options.label: Severe high-gradient AS: proceed to valve intervention
Moderate AS: the low gradient excludes severe AS
Classical low-flow, low-gradient AS: low-dose dobutamine echo to separate true from pseudo-severe AS
Paradoxical low-flow AS with preserved LVEF: CT calcium score

fields.why: Reduced LVEF, SVi ≤ 35 mL/m², AVA < 1.0 cm² and mean gradient < 40 mmHg define classical low-flow, low-gradient AS.

items.concept: Mitral stenosis: MVA = 220 / PHT, heart-rate dependence of the mean gradient, PASP
items.explanation: PHT is the time for the peak transmitral gradient to halve (velocity falls to Vpeak/√2); MVA = 220 / PHT is empirical. It is unreliable when LA or LV compliance is abnormal: immediately after balloon commissurotomy, with significant AR, with LV diastolic dysfunction and in the elderly with calcific (degenerative) MS; planimetry is then the reference. EAE/ASE 2009 severe MS: MVA < 1.0 cm², mean gradient > 10 mmHg, PASP > 50 mmHg. A symptomatic patient with clinically significant MS and favourable anatomy (Wilkins score ≤ 8, no LA thrombus, at most mild MR) is a candidate for percutaneous mitral commissurotomy.

fields.label: MS severity by MVA (EAE/ASE 2009 bands)
fields.why: 0.90 cm² is < 1.0 cm². (ESC/EACTS 2021 and ACC/AHA 2020 call MVA ≤ 1.5 cm² clinically significant or severe, so it is severe by every scheme.)

fields.label: Estimated PASP (no RVOT obstruction)
fields.why: IVC ≤ 2.1 cm but collapsing < 50%: intermediate RA pressure 8 mmHg; PASP = 4 x 3.3² + 8 = 44 + 8 = 52 mmHg.

fields.label: How must the mean gradient be read?

options.label: With the heart rate: tachycardia shortens diastole and raises it (in AF, average 5-10 beats)
On its own: it is independent of heart rate and rhythm
Only the peak gradient matters in mitral stenosis

fields.why: 11 mmHg at 70/min supports severe MS; the same valve in fast AF would show a higher gradient, and a slow rate a lower one, so the MVA is the primary severity measure.

fields.label: Conclusion

options.label: Moderate mitral stenosis without pulmonary hypertension
Functional mitral stenosis from LV dysfunction
Severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with raised pulmonary pressure

fields.why: MVA 0.90 cm², mean gradient 11 mmHg and PASP 52 mmHg are all in the severe range.

items.concept: Mitral regurgitation: vena contracta, PISA EROA, regurgitant volume, pulmonary vein flow
items.explanation: Integrate, do not rely on one number. ASE 2017 severe MR: VC ≥ 0.7 cm, EROA ≥ 0.40 cm², RVol ≥ 60 mL, RF ≥ 50%, plus supportive signs (flail leaflet, dense triangular CW signal, E > 1.2 m/s, systolic flow reversal in more than one pulmonary vein, dilated LA and LV). PISA assumes a hemispheric convergence zone and a round orifice: eccentric jets and wall constraint distort it, and a single-frame PISA overestimates a late-systolic jet. In secondary MR the orifice is often elliptical, so a smaller EROA can already be severe. For severe primary MR, ESC/EACTS 2021 recommends surgery for symptoms, and in asymptomatic patients for LVEF ≤ 60% or LVESD ≥ 40 mm; repair is preferred. ESC/EACTS 2025 adds a class I recommendation for repair in asymptomatic low-risk patients with at least 3 of: AF, SPAP > 50 mmHg, severe LA dilatation (LAVI ≥ 60 mL/m² or LA ≥ 55 mm) and moderate or severe TR (in centres with durable repair results).

fields.label: EROA by PISA
fields.why: Flow = 2π r² x Va = 2π x 0.9² x 40 = 204 mL/s; EROA = 204 / 460 cm/s = 0.44 cm² (severe: ≥ 0.40).

fields.label: Regurgitant volume
fields.why: RVol = EROA x MR VTI = 0.44 x 140 = 62 mL (severe: ≥ 60 mL).

fields.label: Systolic flow reversal in the pulmonary veins

options.label: A specific supportive sign of severe MR
Non-specific: also seen with AF or a high LA pressure of any cause
A sign of coexisting mitral stenosis

fields.why: Systolic reversal means the jet reaches the veins and the LA pressure rises steeply in systole: reversal in more than one pulmonary vein is specific for severe MR, while an eccentric jet can reverse flow in one vein only. Blunting (systolic < diastolic wave) is the non-specific finding, seen with AF or a high LA pressure of any cause.

fields.label: Conclusion
fields.why: Leaflet prolapse (a primary, degenerative lesion), VC ≥ 0.7 cm, EROA ≥ 0.40 cm², RVol ≥ 60 mL and systolic reversal in more than one pulmonary vein all agree: severe primary MR.

measurements.label: Pulmonary vein flow
measurements.value: Systolic flow reversal in the right and left upper veins

items.concept: Aortic regurgitation: PHT, vena contracta, descending aortic flow reversal, volumetric RVol and RF
items.explanation: ASE 2017 severe AR: VC > 0.6 cm, PHT < 200 ms, holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending (better, abdominal) aorta, RVol ≥ 60 mL, RF ≥ 50%, EROA ≥ 0.30 cm², with LV dilatation in chronic AR. The volumetric method works because the LVOT carries forward plus regurgitant flow while the mitral annulus carries forward flow only (valid when MR is no more than mild). Symptoms mean surgery at any LVEF. In asymptomatic severe AR, ESC/EACTS 2021 and 2025 recommend surgery (class I) for LVEF ≤ 50% or LVESD > 50 mm (> 25 mm/m²) and say it may be considered in low-risk patients with LVEF ≤ 55% (IIb; 2025 also lists LVESDi > 22 mm/m² or LVESVi > 45 mL/m²), while ACC/AHA 2020 recommends AVR at LVEF ≤ 55% (class 1) when no other cause explains it. So this asymptomatic patient (LVEF 55%, LVESD 48 mm) sits at a surgical threshold, not simply in follow-up: confirm the LVEF (repeat echo or CMR), index the LV size to body surface area and discuss in the Heart Team. The bicuspid valve also calls for aortic size measurement.

fields.label: Regurgitant volume (volumetric)
fields.why: LVOT SV = π x 1.1² x 39 = 3.80 x 39 = 148 mL (total, includes the regurgitant blood); RVol = 148 - 70 = 78 mL.

fields.label: Pressure half-time of 170 ms
fields.why: A short PHT means rapid equalisation of aortic and LV diastolic pressure. It is load-dependent: a high LV diastolic pressure or vasodilators shorten it, and chronic compensated AR can have a longer one.

fields.label: Conclusion
fields.why: VC > 0.6 cm, PHT < 200 ms, holodiastolic descending aortic reversal, RVol ≥ 60 mL and RF ≥ 50% agree.

measurements.label: Descending aorta
measurements.value: Holodiastolic flow reversal, end-diastolic velocity 24 cm/s

items.concept: Right heart: RVSP = 4V² + RAP, IVC-derived RA pressure, TAPSE, TAPSE/sPAP, ESC/ERS 2022 PH probability
items.explanation: RVSP = 4V²(TR) + RA pressure, and RVSP equals PASP when there is no pulmonary stenosis or RVOT obstruction. RA pressure from the IVC (ASE 2010/2015): ≤ 2.1 cm with > 50% collapse = 3 mmHg, > 2.1 cm with < 50% collapse = 15 mmHg, anything in between = 8 mmHg. ESC/ERS 2022 grade the probability of PH by the TR velocity (≤ 2.8, 2.9-3.4, > 3.4 m/s) plus other signs (RV/LV ratio > 1.0, flattened septum, TAPSE/sPAP < 0.55 mm/mmHg, short RVOT acceleration time, PA dilatation, IVC and RA size). Echo estimates probability; RHC makes the diagnosis. In systemic sclerosis, screening for PAH is part of routine care.

fields.label: Estimated RA pressure (ASE)
fields.why: IVC > 2.1 cm and collapsing < 50% on sniff: high RA pressure, 15 mmHg.

fields.label: RV longitudinal function
fields.why: TAPSE 14 mm is below the 17 mm lower limit (ASE/EACVI 2015).

fields.label: TAPSE / sPAP
fields.why: 14 / 67 = 0.21 mm/mmHg; a low ratio (ESC/ERS 2022 sign < 0.55) means poor RV-arterial coupling.

fields.label: Conclusion

options.label: Low echocardiographic probability of PH, normal RV function
Intermediate probability of PH, normal RV function
High echocardiographic probability of PH with RV dysfunction

fields.why: TR velocity > 3.4 m/s alone gives a high probability of PH (ESC/ERS 2022); reduced TAPSE and a dilated RV add RV dysfunction. Right heart catheterisation confirms PH.

items.concept: Pericardium: effusion size, chamber collapse, IVC plethora, respiratory variation of inflow
items.explanation: Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis supported by echo. In a tight pericardium the two ventricles compete for a fixed volume: inspiration fills the right heart and the septum shifts left, so mitral E falls and tricuspid E rises (the Doppler counterpart of pulsus paradoxus; exaggerated variation is roughly > 25-30% mitral and > 40-60% tricuspid). Collapse appears when intrapericardial pressure exceeds chamber pressure: RA in late diastole/early systole, RV in early diastole. Collapse may be absent with RV hypertrophy or pulmonary hypertension, and may appear early with hypovolaemia (low-pressure tamponade). ESC 2015 sizes: small < 10 mm, moderate 10-20 mm, large > 20 mm.

fields.label: Effusion size (ESC 2015)
fields.why: 23 mm of diastolic echo-free space is a large effusion.

fields.label: Which sign is the most sensitive but the least specific for tamponade?

options.label: RA systolic inversion > 1/3 of the cycle

fields.why: IVC plethora is present in almost every tamponade but also in any raised right-sided pressure; RV early diastolic collapse and RA inversion lasting more than a third of the cycle are the most specific.

fields.label: Conclusion

options.label: Large effusion with echo signs of tamponade physiology
Small effusion, signs explained by pulmonary hypertension

fields.why: Chamber collapse, IVC plethora and exaggerated reciprocal respiratory variation in a hypotensive patient with a raised JVP: tamponade, an indication for urgent pericardiocentesis.

measurements.label: RA wall
measurements.value: Systolic inversion lasting > 1/3 of the cycle

items.concept: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: maximal wall thickness, SAM, resting and provoked LVOT gradient
items.explanation: LVOT obstruction in HCM is dynamic: it rises when preload or afterload falls or contractility rises (Valsalva, standing, exercise, nitrates, dehydration). ESC 2023: obstruction is a peak gradient ≥ 30 mmHg at rest or on provocation, and ≥ 50 mmHg is the haemodynamically important level (the threshold for septal reduction therapy in drug-refractory symptoms). Because a third of patients obstruct only on provocation, a symptomatic patient with a low resting gradient needs Valsalva, standing or exercise echo. The CW signal is late-peaking ('dagger'); take care not to contaminate it with the MR jet. Avoid vasodilators and high-dose diuretics in obstructive HCM; beta-blockers are first line.

fields.label: Resting LVOT peak gradient
fields.why: 4 x 2.0² = 16 mmHg: below 30 mmHg, no resting obstruction.

fields.label: Provoked LVOT peak gradient
fields.why: 4 x 4.2² = 71 mmHg during Valsalva.

fields.label: Septal / posterior wall ratio
fields.why: 21 / 10 = 2.1: asymmetric septal hypertrophy (a ratio ≥ 1.3 is the classic textbook marker).

fields.label: Obstruction category

options.label: Non-obstructive (< 30 mmHg at rest and on provocation)
Latent (provocable): < 30 mmHg at rest, ≥ 30 mmHg on provocation

fields.why: 16 mmHg at rest rising to 71 mmHg with Valsalva: latent (provocable) obstruction, here ≥ 50 mmHg.

fields.label: Conclusion

options.label: HCM with latent LVOT obstruction ≥ 50 mmHg on provocation
Fixed obstruction from valvular aortic stenosis

fields.why: Wall thickness ≥ 15 mm without another cause defines HCM in adults (ESC 2023); the dynamic, late-peaking gradient with SAM is LVOT obstruction, unmasked by provocation.

measurements.label: Mitral valve
measurements.value: SAM with septal contact; posteriorly directed MR jet

items.concept: Prosthetic aortic valve: gradient, DVI, EOA, acceleration time, comparison with the baseline study
items.explanation: A high prosthetic gradient has three explanations: obstruction (low DVI, long AT, rounded jet), patient-prosthesis mismatch (small EOA for body size, but normal DVI and an unchanged gradient since implantation) or high flow (anaemia, fever, regurgitation: normal DVI). The baseline study is the patient's own reference, which is why it is recorded after every valve implantation. ASE 2009 aortic prostheses: peak velocity < 3 / 3-4 / > 4 m/s, mean gradient < 20 / 20-35 / > 35 mmHg, DVI ≥ 0.30 / 0.25-0.29 / < 0.25, AT < 80 / 80-100 / > 100 ms (normal / possible / significant stenosis); the ASE 2024 update keeps this multiparametric approach and adds the AT/ET ratio (> 0.37 favours obstruction). In VARC-3 terms (Généreux et al., 2021), a mean gradient rise ≥ 10 mmHg to ≥ 20 mmHg with a DVI fall ≥ 0.1 from the early post-implant study is moderate haemodynamic valve deterioration, as here (+17 mmHg to 29 mmHg; DVI 0.38 to 0.24). Next: TOE or cardiac CT to separate structural degeneration from thrombus or pannus (leaflet thrombosis may respond to anticoagulation; degeneration may be treated by valve-in-valve TAVI or redo surgery).

fields.label: Effective orifice area
fields.why: EOA = LVOT area x LVOT VTI / jet VTI = π x 1.0² x 18 / 74 = 3.14 x 0.243 = 0.76 cm².
